text: This is the flight deck of a Nimitz-class carrier, drawn to scale. Over the next forty minutes it launches twelve jets, recovers twelve more, and is respotted for the next event. Every coloured dot is a person, and the colour of their jersey says what they are allowed to do.
Start the go. The brown shirts are plane captains. Each one owns a single jet, and stands at its nose through engine start and the control checks.
Two minutes. The shooters point to their wrists, the beacon on the island turns green, and the radio circuits go quiet. From here on, the launch is run almost entirely by hand signal.

Taking tension. Those are the last words spoken until the shot. The green shirts under the nose have fitted the holdback and seated the launch bar in the shuttle. The jet squats onto its nose gear, the pilot goes to military power, cycles the controls, and salutes.

The first shot is the recovery tanker. The catapult officer touches the deck, the deck-edge operator presses fire, and the jet goes from a standstill to about one hundred and fifty knots in two seconds. Everyone within thirty feet is crouched and off the track.

Suspend. A final checker saw one afterburner fail to light and crossed their arms overhead. Nothing fires. The pilot stays at power while the catapult is untensioned, and only then does the shooter step in front with the throttle-back signal. The jet is checked and run again.

Last shot. The waist catapults sit inside the landing area, so they have to be put to bed before anything can land. Shuttles aft, blast deflectors flush, the control bubble lowered and locked. The waist cat officer signals the arresting gear officer with an arm overhead.

Gear manned and ready. The landing signal officers are on their platform at the port quarter, the four cross-deck pendants are set for Hornets, and the crash crane is running. The Air Boss turns the deck green. Ninety-nine, Charlie. Land aircraft.

First trap. The jet is at full power when it touches down, in case the hook misses. Three hundred and fifteen feet later it stops. The hook runner sprints in from the side, the gear puller steps in at the pilot's one o'clock, and the jet turns hard right, folding its wings on the move. It has to be clear of the foul line in under thirty seconds.

Bolter, bolter, bolter. The hook skipped over the wires. Because the pilot never came off the power, the jet simply flies off the angled deck and re-enters the pattern. The landing area is clear again in seconds.

Wave off, foul deck. The jet ahead is still across the foul line, so at half a mile the landing signal officer lights the red wave-off lights. The approaching jet climbs straight ahead over the deck and goes around. This one is not graded.
The last trap is the tanker from the previous event. It launched first, orbited overhead with give-away fuel in case anyone ran low, and lands last.

Recovery complete. Twelve jets recovered in about eleven minutes, including one bolter and one wave-off. The landing area is still clear. Everything that landed is packed onto the bow, nose aft, and chained down.

Respot. The aircraft handler's plan comes off the Ouija board in Flight Deck Control. Tractors peel the bow pack from the back, and each move takes a director, a driver, a brake rider in the cockpit, chock walkers and wing walkers. Six tows at a time, three to six minutes each.
The deck is spotted for the next event. In about forty-five minutes the plane captains will man their jets again, and the whole dance repeats, seven to ten times a day.
